title: Physical and Chemical Changes
seo_title: Primary 5 Basic Science and Technology: Physical and Chemical Changes Worksheets (NERDC)
standard_code: Primary 5 Basic Science and Technology: Living and Non-Living Things
standard_text: Physical changes change the size, shape or state of a material but make no new substance; chemical changes make new substances, shown by colour change, gas, heat or light; some changes can be reversed and others cannot. (summary of the Basic Science and Technology curriculum, Primary 5, theme: Living and Non-Living Things)
meta_desc: Free Primary 5 Basic Science and Technology worksheets (NERDC curriculum, theme: Living and Non-Living Things): physical or chemical?, signs of chemical change, reversible and irreversible, changes in daily life and change investigations. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A chemical change makes a new substance.
key_sub: Physical changes (melting, cutting, dissolving) can often be reversed; chemical changes usually cannot.
body_html:
How to think about it

In a physical change, the substance stays the same. In a chemical change, a new substance forms.

  • Physical changes: melting, freezing, cutting, crushing, dissolving.
  • Chemical changes: burning, rusting, cooking, rotting.
  • Signs of a chemical change: gas bubbles, a new colour or smell, light or heat given off, a solid forming.
Example

Is burning toast physical or chemical?

new black substance

cannot change back

Answer: chemical

Example

Is dissolving salt in water physical or chemical?

evaporate the water to get the salt back

Answer: physical

Common mistakes

  • Thinking every change of colour is a chemical change.
  • Thinking dissolving makes the substance disappear.
  • Thinking chemical changes are always dangerous.

faq.q: How can you tell a chemical change happened?
faq.a: Look for a new substance: bubbles of gas, a new colour or smell, light or heat, or a solid forming in a liquid.
No. Melting changes the state, but the substance is still the same.

faq.q: Why do chemical changes matter for the environment?
faq.a: Burning fuels and some factory processes make pollution, so waste must be treated and reduced.

items.q: Sugar dissolves in water. Why is this a physical change?
c: The sugar is still sugar; the water can evaporate to get it back.
items.e: Dissolving makes a mixture. Evaporate the water and the sugar crystals are left behind.

items.q: Which is a sign that a chemical change may have happened?

items.e: New substances can give off gas, light or heat.

items.q: Which is not a sign of a physical change?

items.e: A new gas from mixing can mean a new substance. Changing shape, size or state are physical changes.

items.q: Salt water is heated until the water is gone and salt is left. What does this show about dissolving salt?
c: It was a physical change: the salt was still there.
items.e: The same salt comes back, so no new substance had formed.

melting is physical, hardening is chemical
items.e: Melting and freezing are changes of state. The chocolate is still chocolate.

items.q: Why is burning dangerous to investigate?
c: It gives out heat and flames that can cause burns and fires.
items.e: Only with adult supervision.

items.q: What is a reversible change?
c: a change that cannot be undone
a change that makes a new material
a change that can be undone, such as melting or dissolving
items.e: No new material.

items.q: What is an irreversible change?
c: a change that makes a new material and cannot easily be undone
items.e: Burning, cooking, rusting.

items.q: What happens when vinegar is added to bicarbonate of soda?
c: It turns into salt water only.
It fizzes and makes carbon dioxide gas.
items.e: A new gas is made.

items.q: Is melting chocolate reversible?
c: No, it makes a new material.
Yes, it sets again when it cools.
items.e: Change of state.

items.q: Sand and iron filings are mixed. Which shows the mixing was a physical change?
c: A magnet can pull the iron filings back out.
items.e: If you can separate the parts and they are unchanged, no new substance formed.

items.q: Water boils and bubbles form. Is this evidence of a new substance?
c: No. The bubbles are water vapour, the same substance as a gas.
Yes, the bubbles are a new gas.
items.e: Boiling is a change of state. The bubbles are water in its gas form.

items.q: Why is recycling aluminium cans useful?
c: Melting and reshaping cans uses less energy than mining new aluminium.
items.e: Recycling is a physical change that saves resources.

items.q: Obinna wants to find out which liquid makes iron nails rust fastest. What should he keep the same?

items.q: Abdullahi dissolves sugar in warm and cold water. Which is a fair way to compare them?
c: use different cups of different sizes
use the same amount of sugar, water and stirring
use more sugar in the cold water
items.e: Change only the temperature.

items.q: A sealed bag holds 100 g of vinegar and a small cup with 20 g of baking soda. The bag is tipped so they mix and the bag puffs up. What is the total mass now?
items.e: A new gas forms, but the bag is sealed, so nothing gets out: 100 + 20 = 120 g. The particles are rearranged, not destroyed.

items.q: How are iron railings stopped from rusting?
c: painting or oiling them to keep water and air away
items.e: Barrier methods.

items.q: Which safety rule is most important when testing mixtures in class?
c: Wear safety goggles and never taste the mixtures.
Mix as many things as possible.
items.e: Unknown mixtures can be harmful. Goggles protect your eyes, and you should never taste them.

items.q: Nkechi mixes two liquids and sees no bubbles, no colour change and no temperature change. Can she be sure no new substance formed?
c: Not completely; she can test more properties of the mixture.
No, a new substance always forms.
items.e: Not every chemical change is easy to see. More tests (like testing with a magnet or heating) can give more evidence.

items.q: Hauwa heats 20 g of chocolate until it melts, then cools it. It weighs 20 g again. What does this show?
c: Melting is reversible and no material is lost.

items.e: The same material changed state.

items.q: A student says that burning paper is a physical change because the ashes are still paper. Which evidence shows the student is wrong?
c: Ash, smoke and gases have different properties from paper, and they cannot turn back into paper.
items.e: Burning makes new substances. Ash cannot be made back into a sheet of paper.

items.q: Why might baking powder in a cake mixture make the cake rise?
